name: Relamorelin

lead: Relamorelin (RM-131) is an investigational injected ghrelin analogue. Some people group it with ghrelin-pathway compounds associated with appetite, growth hormone and lean mass.

It is a synthetic pentapeptide that activates the ghrelin receptor, which raises growth hormone and appetite. It was developed to speed stomach emptying in diabetic gastroparesis, and phase 2 trials reported faster emptying and less vomiting. It was also studied in constipation and anorexia nervosa. Phase 3 trials registered in 2017 and 2018 were all later terminated.

paras: It has been given as a subcutaneous injection inside clinical trials only. It is not sold as a product.
It is not approved anywhere. Safety data come from clinical trials in gastrointestinal and eating-disorder patients, and no studies have tested it for appearance.

angle.text: Relamorelin activates the ghrelin receptor to raise appetite and growth hormone signalling, and some link that to more lean mass and a fuller look. It was studied for diabetic gastroparesis, and no appearance data exist.

lead: Relamorelin (RM-131, BIM-28131) is a synthetic pentapeptide that mimics ghrelin, the gut hormone that stimulates appetite and growth hormone release, and is given by subcutaneous injection. It was developed as a prokinetic for diabetic gastroparesis, a condition of delayed stomach emptying, and was also tested in chronic constipation, constipation in Parkinson disease and anorexia nervosa.[1][2][3]

The appearance-related angle is the ghrelin pathway: ghrelin receptor agonists raise appetite, growth hormone and related hormones, and in the one small trial in anorexia nervosa relamorelin was associated with a trend toward weight gain over four weeks.[1][4] Researchers describing the drug class link ghrelin signalling to eating behaviour, gastric motility and nausea.[5] Relamorelin itself has been studied only in patients under clinical-trial conditions; no study has tested it for muscle building or physique goals.

Phase 2 trials in diabetic gastroparesis reported faster gastric emptying and symptom reductions, and a 2023 meta-analysis of five randomised trials (1,033 participants) found a modest but statistically significant improvement in gastric emptying time.[2][3][6] Five phase 3 studies were registered in 2017-2018 and are all listed as terminated, and Wikipedia describes the drug's development status as uncertain.[1][7][8][9][10][11]
infobox: FDA Fast Track for diabetic gastroparesis[1]

paras: Relamorelin is not an approved medicine. Its main development target was diabetic gastroparesis, in which stomach emptying is slowed and people experience nausea, vomiting, bloating, early fullness and pain.[12] When the drug was in development, metoclopramide was the only approved gastroparesis medicine in the United States, and reviewers listed relamorelin among the newer prokinetics under evaluation.[12][13]

The same prokinetic action in the colon led to trials in chronic constipation and in constipation associated with Parkinson disease, and the appetite-stimulating action of ghrelin led to a pilot programme in anorexia nervosa.[14][15][16][4][17]

Ghrelin is often called the hunger hormone, and ghrelin receptor agonists increase appetite and growth hormone secretion.[1][5] For people interested in gaining weight or muscle, that is the theoretical link: more appetite and a higher growth hormone signal. Relamorelin has not been tested in healthy people or athletes for this purpose, and no human data exist on lean mass or physique. The only weight data come from an anorexia nervosa trial, where participants who took it were reported to feel more hungry, and some stopped treatment because of that hunger.[4]

Ghrelin was identified in 1999 by Masayasu Kojima, Kenji Kangawa and colleagues as a stomach-derived peptide that releases growth hormone through the receptor GHS-R1a, which is where the name comes from.[18] It is made mainly by endocrine cells in the stomach and upper intestine, rises before meals and falls afterwards, and is widely known as the hunger hormone. Injected ghrelin increases food intake in humans, largely by prompting more meals rather than larger ones, and synthetic ghrelin mimetics are reported to increase body weight and fat mass.[18]

Because native ghrelin is quickly broken down, drug developers have pursued longer-acting analogues such as relamorelin. Ghrelin also speeds gastric motility, which is why a stable analogue was tested as a treatment for stomach-emptying disorders and not only for appetite.[18][5]

Gastroparesis is a condition in which weak stomach contractions leave food in the stomach too long. Autonomic nerve damage affecting the vagus nerve, seen in roughly 30 to 50 percent of people with long-standing diabetes, is the best-known cause, and typical symptoms are nausea, vomiting, early fullness, bloating and abdominal pain.[19] Existing options include dietary changes, metoclopramide (which carries a boxed warning for tardive dyskinesia), erythromycin and, in refractory cases, gastric electrical stimulation, which left room for new prokinetics to be evaluated.[19]

Relamorelin is a centrally penetrant, selective agonist of the ghrelin receptor (growth hormone secretagogue receptor 1a) with improved potency and pharmacokinetic properties compared with native ghrelin.[1][20] Ghrelin and the related hormone motilin are produced mainly in the gut. Ghrelin raises appetite and hedonic eating, and both hormones act on structurally similar receptors that have been explored as targets for gastrointestinal disorders.[5]

In humans, ghrelin receptor agonists raise growth hormone, prolactin and cortisol and increase appetite.[1] Because ghrelin receptors are also found in the colon, researchers hypothesised that the drug could speed colonic transit as well as gastric emptying.[17] In healthy volunteers, relamorelin affected gastric motor functions and satiation.[21]
Relamorelin is a synthetic pentapeptide, a five-amino-acid chain engineered as an analogue of ghrelin, with the molecular formula C43H50N8O5S.[1]

A phase 2a trial in 204 patients with diabetic gastroparesis reported that relamorelin reduced the frequency and severity of vomiting and accelerated gastric emptying.[2] A 12-week phase 2b trial randomised 393 patients (mostly type 2 diabetes, median age 58) to placebo or one of three relamorelin dose groups. Vomiting frequency fell by about 75 percent from baseline, but that reduction was not significantly different from the placebo group. The four core symptoms (nausea, abdominal pain, postprandial fullness and bloating) and a composite symptom score were significantly reduced in all relamorelin groups compared with placebo, and gastric emptying was accelerated.[3][22]

A combined safety analysis of the two phase 2 trials found similar proportions of serious adverse events across treatment groups, with more discontinuations because of adverse events in the relamorelin groups. One death in the phase 2b trial, from urosepsis, was judged unrelated to the drug. HbA1c and fasting blood glucose rose in a dose-related way in the phase 2b trial, and the authors concluded that blood glucose should be managed proactively in treated patients.[23]

A 2023 meta-analysis of five randomised trials with 1,033 participants found gastric emptying time improved by 11.4 minutes compared with placebo (8.4 minutes in the diabetic subgroup). Headache, dizziness and gastrointestinal symptoms were more common in the relamorelin group.[6]
Five phase 3 studies in diabetic gastroparesis, enrolling between 202 and 467 participants each, began between September 2017 and December 2018 and are all listed as terminated.[7][8][9][10][11]

In a randomised trial of 48 women with chronic constipation, two weeks of relamorelin accelerated gastric emptying and colonic transit compared with placebo and increased spontaneous bowel movements.[17] A separate short randomised trial examined its effects on descending-colon motility.[14] A trial in Parkinson disease with constipation (MOVE-PD) completed only 18 of 56 intended participants, in part because many patients turned out to have multiple partially complete bowel movements that made them ineligible. The investigators said this recruitment shortfall prevented any conclusion about benefit.[24][15]

A randomised, double-blind trial at Massachusetts General Hospital gave relamorelin or placebo for four weeks to 22 outpatient women with anorexia nervosa. Weight rose by about 0.86 kg on relamorelin versus 0.04 kg on placebo, a difference the authors described as a trend (p = 0.07), and gastric emptying time was significantly shorter. Three participants on relamorelin stopped because of increased hunger. The authors called for longer studies.[4][16]
A phase 1 study in 16 healthy volunteers examined effects on satiation, gastric volume and accommodation, and reported effects on gastric motor functions and satiation.[21]

Across diabetic gastroparesis trials, headache, dizziness and gastrointestinal symptoms were more common with relamorelin than placebo, and adverse-event discontinuations were proportionally higher in the treated groups.[6][23] Dose-related increases in HbA1c and fasting glucose were seen in the phase 2b study.[23] Increased hunger led some anorexia nervosa participants to withdraw.[4] Safety data come only from clinical trials in patient populations.

Relamorelin was developed by Rhythm Pharmaceuticals and later held by Allergan, and the FDA granted Fast Track designation for diabetic gastroparesis.[1] A phase 1b study in women with type 2 diabetes and delayed gastric emptying was reported in 2013.[1] Phase 2 results in diabetic gastroparesis were published in 2016 and 2017, and phase 3 studies were registered in 2017-2018.[2][3][7]
Wikipedia notes that a 2019 company filing listed an expected 2024 launch that did not appear in later filings, and describes the drug's development as uncertain.[1]
